import { Steps, Aside, Tabs, TabItem, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import SeqDiagram from '../../../components/SeqDiagram.astro';

This tutorial walks one path from nothing to a running key-value app. You will
write a small Rust crate, build it to WebAssembly, install it on a cluster,
create an instance of it (a context), and call its methods, checking the
output at each step.

The worked example mirrors the in-repo [`apps/kv-store`](/build/examples/) app,
trimmed to the parts you need the first time through. When you finish you will
have a context whose state you and the people you invite can read and write
from the command line.

<Aside type="note">
  The Rust code, the build command, and the `meroctl` flags here are taken from
  the in-repo example (`apps/kv-store/`) and the CLI definitions
  (`crates/meroctl/src`). Run `meroctl <command> --help` to confirm them for
  your build; every command is in the [meroctl reference](/operate/meroctl/).
</Aside>

## 1. Prerequisites

<Steps>

1. **The `cargo mero` toolchain.** It scaffolds, builds, tests, and bundles
   Calimero apps:

   ```sh
   cargo install cargo-mero
   ```

   See [the cargo mero toolchain](/build/cargo-mero/) for other install methods.
   `cargo mero build` auto-installs the `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target and has
   `wasm-opt` built in, so there is nothing else to set up.

2. **A development cluster.** `merod local` runs three nodes in one process,
   with mock attestation; save its first node in `meroctl` and sign in with a
   passkey kept in a file (development clusters only):

   ```sh
   merod local
   # in another terminal
   meroctl node add local http://127.0.0.1:2501/ --allow-mock
   meroctl login --dev-passkey ./dev-passkey.json --name alice
   ```

   `login` signs up when the file does not exist yet, and saves the session.
   See [Run local nodes](/contribute/development/#run-local-nodes).

</Steps>

## 2. Create the project

<Steps>

1. Scaffold the app:

   ```sh
   cargo mero new kv-store
   cd kv-store
   ```

   This writes a ready-to-build crate: `Cargo.toml`, `src/lib.rs`
   (a working state + logic + a `#[cfg(test)]` TestHost test),
   `tests/converge.rs`, and `GUIDE.md` (the app's guide for agents, with
   the five sections the registry requires).

2. Open the generated `Cargo.toml`. The load-bearing parts `cargo mero new`
   wrote for you:

   ```toml
   [lib]
   # cdylib is the wasm the node loads; rlib lets `cargo test` link the app.
   crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]

   [dependencies]
   thiserror = "1"
   # SDK crates pinned to a git tag.
   calimero-sdk = { git = "https://github.com/calimero-network/core", tag = "<sdk-tag>" }
   calimero-storage = { git = "https://github.com/calimero-network/core", tag = "<sdk-tag>" }

   [dev-dependencies]
   # Native test harness (TestHost) + CRDT merge under `cargo test`.
   calimero-storage = { git = "https://github.com/calimero-network/core", tag = "<sdk-tag>", features = ["testing"] }

   [package.metadata.calimero]
   # Reverse-DNS app id the node installs the bundle under.
   package = "com.example.kv-store"
   name = "kv-store"

   # cargo mero build compiles under this; --profiling uses app-profiling instead.
   [profile.app-release]
   inherits = "release"
   opt-level = "z"      # optimize for size: wasm ships over the wire
   lto = true
   panic = "abort"      # no unwinding in wasm
   overflow-checks = true

   # Empty [workspace] makes this crate its own workspace root, so cargo reads
   # the app-* profiles (which only apply at a workspace root).
   [workspace]
   ```

   The `[package.metadata.calimero]` table is your bundle identity; the full set
   of keys is in the [toolchain metadata reference](/build/cargo-mero/#metadata-reference).

3. Open `src/lib.rs`. The scaffold already put a working key-value app there.
   The next sections walk through the shape it follows so you can change it with
   confidence; every app starts from the same imports:

   ```rust
   use calimero_sdk::app;
   use calimero_storage::collections::{LwwRegister, UnorderedMap};
   ```

</Steps>

## 3. Define the state

Your app's persistent state is a single struct annotated with `#[app::state]`.
Its fields are CRDT [collections](/build/collections/) — replicated types that
merge cleanly when two nodes change them concurrently.

Here the state is a map from `String` keys to `LwwRegister<String>` values. An
`LwwRegister` ("last-writer-wins") holds one value and keeps the most recent
write when nodes diverge.

```rust
#[app::state(emits = for<'a> Event<'a>)]
pub struct KvStore {
    items: UnorderedMap<String, LwwRegister<String>>,
}
```

The `emits = ...` part declares that this app emits the `Event` type you define
next. If your app does not emit events, you can write just `#[app::state]`.

## 4. Add logic and events

<Steps>

1. Declare the events your app emits with `#[app::event]`. Events are how an app
   tells the outside world what changed — clients can subscribe to them:

   ```rust
   #[app::event]
   pub enum Event<'a> {
       Inserted { key: &'a str, value: &'a str },
       Updated { key: &'a str, value: &'a str },
   }
   ```

2. Add the logic block. Every app needs exactly one `#[app::init]` that returns
   the initial state. Then add a setter that mutates state (`&mut self`) and a
   getter that only reads it (`&self`):

   ```rust
   #[app::logic]
   impl KvStore {
       #[app::init]
       pub fn init() -> KvStore {
           KvStore {
               items: UnorderedMap::new(),
           }
       }

       pub fn set(&mut self, key: String, value: String) -> app::Result<()> {
           app::log!("Setting key: {:?} to value: {:?}", key, value);

           if self.items.contains(&key)? {
               app::emit!(Event::Updated { key: &key, value: &value });
           } else {
               app::emit!(Event::Inserted { key: &key, value: &value });
           }

           self.items.insert(key, value.into())?;
           Ok(())
       }

       pub fn get(&self, key: &str) -> app::Result<Option<String>> {
           app::log!("Getting key: {:?}", key);
           Ok(self.items.get(key)?.map(|v| v.get().clone()))
       }
   }
   ```

   A few things to notice, all real SDK API:

   - `app::log!` writes to the node's execution log.
   - `app::emit!` emits one of your declared events.
   - Collection calls (`contains`, `insert`, `get`) return `Result`, so they
     end in `?`.
   - `value.into()` turns the `String` into an `LwwRegister<String>`; `v.get()`
     reads the register's current value back out.

</Steps>

<Aside type="tip" title="Test before you build">
  The SDK ships a native in-process harness — `calimero_sdk::testing::TestHost`,
  enabled by the `calimero-storage` `testing` feature the scaffold put under
  `[dev-dependencies]`. You can drive your methods and assert on state under
  `cargo mero test` (or plain `cargo test`), with no node and no WASM build:

  ```rust
  #[cfg(test)]
  mod tests {
      use calimero_sdk::testing::TestHost;
      use super::*;

      #[test]
      fn set_then_get() {
          let mut app = TestHost::new(KvStore::init);
          app.call(|s| s.set("k".into(), "v".into())).unwrap();
          assert_eq!(app.view(|s| s.get("k")).unwrap(), Some("v".to_owned()));
      }
  }
  ```
</Aside>

## 5. Build and package

Build the app with one command:

```sh
cargo mero build
```

It compiles to `wasm32-unknown-unknown` under the `app-release` profile,
size-optimizes with `wasm-opt -Oz`, and embeds the ABI. The artifact lands at:

```
res/kv_store.wasm
```

:::note
The filename is the crate name with hyphens turned into underscores — crate
`kv-store` produces `kv_store.wasm`.
:::

A node installs only a signed bundle, so package the wasm into one:

```sh
cargo mero bundle --dev --no-icon
```

```
dist/com.example.kv-store-0.1.0.mpk
```

The name is the manifest's `package` and `version`, not the crate name.

## 6. Install and run

`meroctl` sends every request through the sealed channel to the node it saved,
after checking the node's attestation. Its output is JSON.

<Steps>

1. **Install** the signed bundle on the cluster. Uploading a bundle is for
   development clusters; a production cluster installs a release from its
   registry (`meroctl app install com.example.kv-store@0.1.0`):

   ```sh
   meroctl app install --path ./dist/com.example.kv-store-0.1.0.mpk
   meroctl app ls
   ```

2. **Create a context**: an instance of your app with its own state, replicated
   on three nodes. Its `init` runs once, now. `--alias` names it for your
   account:

   ```sh
   meroctl context create --name my-kv --package com.example.kv-store --alias my-kv
   ```

   ```json
   { "appId": "…", "contextId": "…", "group": 7, "replicas": [1, 2, 3] }
   ```

3. **Call the setter** to write a key. `--args` is JSON matching the method's
   parameters:

   ```sh
   meroctl call -c my-kv set --args '{"key": "hello", "value": "world"}'
   ```

   ```json
   { "index": 2, "result": null, "events": [{ "kind": "Inserted", "data": { "key": "hello", "value": "world" } }], "receipt": { … } }
   ```

   `set` returns `()`, so `result` is `null`. `index` is the entry's position in
   the context's log, and `receipt` is the answering node's signature over the
   result.

4. **Call the getter** to read it back. `--view` reads without writing:

   ```sh
   meroctl call -c my-kv get --args '{"key": "hello"}' --view
   ```

   ```json
   { "index": 2, "result": "world", "receipt": { … } }
   ```

   The value you stored comes back as `result`. Your first app works.

</Steps>

Here is what that `call set` does once it reaches the cluster: the node checks
your session and your access, the context's leader runs the method, and the
other replicas apply what it wrote:

<SeqDiagram id="d-build-tutorial-exec" title="One method, end to end"
  lanes={[
    { label: 'meroctl', color: '#3fb950' },
    { label: 'Any node', color: '#58a6ff' },
    { label: 'Leader (WASM)', color: '#a371f7' },
    { label: 'Replicas', color: '#39d0d8' },
  ]}
  steps={[
    { from: 0, to: 1, label: 'sealed POST /apps/{app}/intents set {key, value}' },
    { from: 1, to: 1, label: 'session + access, on fresh system state' },
    { from: 1, to: 2, label: 'forward to the context\'s leader' },
    { from: 2, to: 2, label: 'run set: insert into UnorderedMap, emit Inserted' },
    { from: 2, to: 3, label: 'append { call, outcome } to the log' },
    { from: 3, to: 2, label: 'majority holds it: committed', dashed: true },
    { from: 2, to: 1, label: 'result + events', dashed: true },
    { from: 1, to: 0, label: 'answer + signed receipt', dashed: true },
  ]} />

## 7. Make it multi-user

A context belongs to an organization, and everyone in it reaches the context.
Create one, create the context in it, and invite a second person:

<Steps>

1. **Create an organization** and a context in it:

   ```sh
   meroctl namespace create acme
   meroctl context create --name team-kv --package com.example.kv-store \
     --namespace <org-id> --alias team-kv
   ```

   A context created in an organization is reached by every member (access
   `org`, the default there).

2. **Invite** a member. The command prints an invitation token:

   ```sh
   meroctl namespace invite <org-id> --role member
   ```

3. **Join** as the second person: a second account, with its own passkey file,
   on the same cluster. Save the node under another `--home` so the two sessions
   stay apart:

   ```sh
   meroctl --home ./bob node add local http://127.0.0.1:2501/ --allow-mock
   meroctl --home ./bob login --dev-passkey ./bob-passkey.json --name bob
   meroctl --home ./bob namespace join <token>
   ```

4. **Write as one, read as the other**:

   ```sh
   meroctl --home ./bob call -c <context-id> set --args '{"key": "from", "value": "bob"}'
   meroctl call -c team-kv get --args '{"key": "from"}' --view
   ```

   ```json
   { "index": 2, "result": "bob", "receipt": { … } }
   ```

</Steps>

Both people wrote and read the same state, each with their own passkey, through
any node of the cluster. The organization decides who reaches the context;
what each member may change inside it is the app's own code and its
[access-controlled storage](/build/permissioned-storage/). See
[Organizations, teams & access](/protocol/organizations/).
